Comment on today’s Mini:  HAIL is not technically frozen rain.  

Pedantic summary of some of my least favourite weather types courtesy of Google :)

• Hail forms inside cumulonimbus thunderstorm clouds, where strong upward-moving air currents (updrafts) carry water droplets high above the freezing level. As these droplets freeze and bounce around the cloud, they collect more supercooled water, building up solid layers of ice until they become too heavy for the updraft and fall to the ground.

• Freezing rain starts as snow or ice melting into liquid rain as it falls through a warm layer of air, and then hits a sub-freezing surface on or near the ground, turning into a glaze of ice upon impact.

• Sleet (ice pellets) also starts as snow that melts into rain in a warm layer, but it refreezes into tiny solid ice pellets while still in the air before hitting the ground.

There is a programming glitch with the cats. We had the puzzle solved correctly but it wouldn't solve officially. Unbeknownst to us, there was a letter typed into the cat boxes, hidden because the cats were sitting on top of them! The puzzle either came that way, or we unknowingly typed letters into both cat squares. (Unlikely.) I can't think of a more frustrating puzzle than one in which you KNOW it's solved, but the program disagrees. It's like arguing with HAL. 

We finally solved it by searching online for a trick with the Midi for today and found a comment from someone who said he had to enter a CAT rebus and then erase it to get the puzzle to solve. ORA has been an answer in 657 puzzles, going all the way back to 1942. UMA - 200 times, also going back to 1942. 

They are just useful pieces of fill to connect the more useful answers in the puzzle. As another example - OREO has been an answer 526 times, though in pre-Shortz puzzles it was always clued as "Mountain: Comb. form" (or "Prefix "). 

Kind of interesting that that changed completely starting in the Shortz era. That seems to indicate that there was a significant change in the rules at that point. I might do some other answer history searches to see if I can confirm that.

Gatling guns from the 1920's and 1930's gangsters during Prohibition  in the US (from selling alcohol)  are shortened to "gats" often in crossword puzzles.
GAT has been used in more than crossword puzzles. https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/gat
It is a slang word for gun.  I had to look it up as I am not with the gun mentality.    .... "gats"

A Gatling gun is a very heavy, hand-cranked gun on wheels, dating to the civil war; I think they were obsolete by WWI.

The stereotypical gangster weapon is the Thompson submachine gun (aka the "Tommy").

Gatling guns inspired the design for Tommy guns and many other firearms. The term gat is still commonly used to refer to hand held firearms in general, particularly in street gang culture and gangster rap.
I learned GAT as a kid, when we all watched gangster movies and read Dick Tracy in the comics.

It seems that the progression was that the term GAT originally referred specifically referred to a type of gun that become obsolete, so the slang meaning drifted to denote any kind of handgun (see Barry's link).

So there's no need to debate whether 1920s gangsters used actual Gatlin guns.
